brand.title: The Infrastructure of Black Chicago: The Institutions, Places, Networks and People That Built a Cultural Metropolis

note: ONLY verified relationships. Types per CTL-DR-BCI-001 prompt.

relationships.evidence: BlackPast.org: Abbott founded and published the Chicago Defender, first issue May 6, 1905; NMAAHC confirms Abbott's founding role.
NMAAHC: the Defender was located at 34th Street and Indiana Avenue on the South Side, 'Locals called the neighborhood "Bronzeville."'
NPR/WCMU (2022): 'Black Americans began arriving on these blocks in 1916 as part of the Great Migration'; by the 1920s they had built the Bronzeville community.

Capital University Law Review: Hansberry bought a house in the South Park subdivision in 1937, 'an allwhite territory surrounded by black communities,' which served as 'a blockade against encroachment by the black ghetto into white Woodlawn on the east.'
Wikipedia (Ida B. Wells Homes): the project was a CHA public housing project 'in the Bronzeville neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago.'

Wikipedia (Ida B. Wells Homes): 'a Chicago Housing Authority (CHA) public housing project in the Bronzeville neighborhood,' bounded by 35th Street, Pershing Road, King Drive, and Cottage Grove Avenue.
Wikipedia (Contract Buyers League): 'formed in 1968 by residents of North Lawndale'; Chicago Reporter: first meeting January 1968 in Lawndale; meetings at Presentation Catholic Church.
Bill Moyers/Coates (2014): Ross joined the CBL in 1968 to fight contract sellers; Chicago Catholic (2017): Ross served as co-chairman of the newly formed Contract Buyers League.
The Citizen Newspaper Group (2013): on January 26, 1966 King moved to a third-floor apartment at 1550 South Hamlin in North Lawndale.
Wikipedia (Marquette Park rallies): on August 5, 1966 King led 700 marchers through Marquette Park and Gage Park, where he was struck in the head with a rock.

Middlebury project: King 'moved into an apartment at 1550 South Hamlin Avenue in North Lawndale' as the base of the Chicago campaign; the movement 'assumed trusteeship' of a building at 1321 South Homan Avenue in February 1966.
Illinois Secretary of State memorial resolution (1988): Washington 'grew up in the Bronzeville neighborhood on the city's South Side.'
AAIHS: the University of Chicago sponsored the Hyde Park–Kenwood Urban Renewal Plan, approved by the city in 1958, covering 856 acres with 638 buildings demolished and 4,000 families displaced.
Barnett founded the Associated Negro Press March 2, 1919 (Wikipedia; Stanford King Institute; Nieman Reports).
Johnson founded Johnson Publishing Company in 1942 (Chicago Architecture Center; Smithsonian NMAAHC).
Jackson pastored Olivet 1941–1990 (Encyclopedia of Chicago / Chicago Historical Society ICHi-37946).
Dyett ran the renowned music program at DuSable (City of Chicago landmark report).
Cornelius created Soul Train, premiered on WCIU-TV Aug 17, 1970 (Wikipedia; Chicago City Council proclamation 2025).
Cornelius was a newsreader and backup disc jockey at WVON before WCIU (Wikipedia Soul Train; BET).
Johnson graduated DuSable High School with honors (Chicago Architecture Center; Wikipedia).
Brooks was in Wilson Junior College's first graduating class, 1936 (City Colleges of Chicago Special Collections).

relationships.evidence: The Business History Review documents Gillespie heading the investment group that incorporated the company in 1919.
Institutional histories document Williams's 1891 founding of Provident Hospital.
CPL's archives blog and the BMRC exhibit text document the 1975 transfer of Harsh's collection to Woodson and its renaming.
Margaret Taylor-Burroughs co-founded the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art (now DuSable) in 1961 and served as executive director for its first ten years.
Burroughs was a key member of the Community Art Center Committee that raised funds for SSCAC's 1940 opening; DuSable CEO Perri Irmer calls SSCAC one of 'both of her wonderful institutions.'
Located at 3533 S. Giles Ave in the Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District; listed in the 'Black Metropolis TR' (thematic resource) on the National Register.
Erected 1927 by the State of Illinois in Bronzeville, home of the 'Fighting Eighth' Regiment; at 35th & King Drive, south end of the Bronzeville Walk of Fame.
At 3435 S. Indiana Ave in the Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District; housed the Chicago Defender 1920-1960.
3831 S. Michigan Ave, Bronzeville; founded 1940 as WPA art center serving the Black Belt.
